title: The body is on loan
hookLine: Epictetus lists even the body among things not fully ours (Enchiridion 1)

lines: WHAT IF THE BODY IS BORROWED?
cards: A friend lends you her car for the weekend, and something changes in the driver's seat. The fries stay in the bag. The mirrors get checked twice.
The tank goes back full, maybe after a trip through the car wash. Nobody asked for any of it. A borrowed thing gets a different kind of care.
Now a strange thought from Epictetus, the last of our week on control: what if your body is more like the borrowed car than one you own?

teach.h: FIRST ON THE NOT-MINE LIST: THE BODY.
teach.b: Go back to the first lines of the Handbook: some things are up to us, some are not. The very first thing on the not-up-to-us list is the body. That sounds wrong.
My body is the most mine thing there is. But look at it the way Epictetus did. You didn't choose its height, or its genes, or when it catches a cold.
You can't order your knee to stop hurting or your hair to stay. It ages on its own schedule. You live in it, you steer it, you're responsible for it.

teach.h: YOU STEER IT; YOU DON'T COMMAND IT.
teach.b: But you don't fully command it. Later in the Handbook, he gives the picture that goes with this.
Never say of anything, I have lost it, he says, in paraphrase; say instead, I have given it back.
What we have is given for a time, like a traveler's room at an inn: use it well while you're there, and don't pretend it's yours forever. Here's the surprise. This isn't a reason to neglect the body.
It's the reason to care for it well. The borrowed car gets the careful driving. Sleep, water, a walk, the vegetables, the checkup: not vanity, and not punishment.

teach.h: CARE FOR IT LIKE A BORROWED THING.
teach.b: That's how a good guest treats a borrowed thing.
And the loan helps with the other side too. When the knee hurts or the mirror shows a new gray hair, you can meet it with less outrage. That part was never yours to command.
What's yours is how you care for it, and how you meet what it does.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism treat the body as not fully theirs, following Enchiridion 1 and 11: they care for it steadily and try to meet illness and aging without outrage.

o: Epictetus's short book of Stoic teaching
a Greek doctor's guide to the body
a manual of rules for Roman soldiers

games.q: what's inside the loan — tap the pairs.
p: say instead: I have given it back
use the room well while you're there
how a good guest treats a borrowed thing

s: Epictetus puts the body among the things up to us
the body is the very first thing on his not-up-to-us list.
Epictetus says to say I have given it back, not I have lost it
the things we have are given for a time.
if the body isn't fully yours, there's no point caring for it
the opposite: Epictetus says to care for it as a thing that belongs to another.

games.q: you notice a new ache that won't go away. following this week's Stoic sorting, what do you do?
o: rage at your body for letting you down.
ignore it, since the body isn't yours anyway.
meet it calmly, and do your part: rest, or see a doctor.
games.why: the ache was never yours to command. your care and your response are, so you do your part and let go of the outrage.

practice: Move your attention slowly through the body, feet, legs, belly, chest, hands, shoulders, face, and look it over the way you'd look over a borrowed car: with interest, not judgment. Where is it tired, and where does it ache?
Then ask what one thing a good guest would do for it, water, sleep, a stretch, a walk, and breathe with that choice.

wordCard.voice: Handbook. Epictetus's book, where the body is listed among things not fully ours, which is why it deserves careful keeping. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: the body. In Enchiridion 1 it is the first thing on the list of what is not up to us.

carryVoice: Your line: on loan. From mine or not mine to on loan, the week's six lines all ask the same question. A new week, on gratitude, starts tomorrow.
